Thank you, Renato. That was clear, and you finished in eleven minutes, so you did not run over. Now let me ask the questions my team will ask.
Of course. I am ready.
You said units in the South fell in the third quarter. Why should we believe the recovery plan?
Because we have already started it. We did joint visits to both clinics, and one doctor told us she would come back in December.
Good answer. But you rushed it. Slow down your pace when you give a number.
Fair point. I will pause after every number.
Next question. What do you need from the global team?
One thing: six weeks of stock in the South, and a weekly call with the supply team.
That is a strong closing line. Use it at the end, not in the middle.
Understood. And the opening? I used a cue card.
Keep the card, but look up. Eye contact is half of the message. The rehearsal is over. Next week, you do it for real.

Hi Renato, it is Claire. A few notes before your presentation next week. You have fifteen minutes, so please talk for twelve and leave three for questions. Last year, two managers ran over, and we had no time for questions, which is the part I care about most. Start with a hook, not with the agenda. My team will be on the call from four countries, and some of them are not native speakers either, so a slower pace is a gift, not a weakness. Pause after every number, because people need two seconds to write it down. Do not read your slides. I would rather see you look at the camera with a cue card in your hand. And please prepare for three hard questions: the drop in the South, the recovery plan, and what you need from us. If you finish with one clear request, I can usually say yes on the same call. Good luck. I am looking forward to it.

The first time I presented to the global team in English, I was so nervous that I finished a twenty-minute presentation in eleven minutes. I rushed every slide. My director told me later that nobody understood my numbers, because I said them too fast. My nerves also produced filler words. I said so, and, um, maybe forty times. For the second presentation, I changed three things. First, I did the rehearsal out loud, five times, standing up, with a timer. Second, I wrote my opening and my closing line on a cue card, word for word, because those are the moments when the nerves are worst. Third, I recorded myself and counted my filler words. The number went down from forty to six. My body language changed too. I stopped holding the table. The presentation was not perfect, but at the end the vice president asked me two questions, and that is how I knew they were really listening.

Good morning, and thank you for your time. Last year, my team grew market share by three percentage points. Today I will walk you through our results, one problem, and our plan. To close, I will ask you for one thing.
